blocks.text: Fig 15.14 shows the convex surface of a lens in contact with a plane glass plate. A thin film of air is formed between the two surfaces. When we view the setup with monochromatic light, you see circular interference fringes (Fig.15.15). These were studied by Newton and are called Newton's rings.

blocks.alt: A plano-convex lens, flat side up, rests on a flat glass plate and touches it at the centre. Near the edge a ray comes down and two rays, reflected from the top and bottom of the thin air film of thickness t, go up to an eye.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.14: Convex lens in contact with glass plate (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.14).

blocks.alt: A circular field of view showing concentric dark and bright rings with a dark spot at the centre; the rings get closer together further from the centre.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.15: Circular interference fringes (original drawing after the textbook's photograph, Figure 15.15).

blocks.text: Newton's rings are formed when a plano-convex lens is placed on a flat glass plate, a thin air film forms between them. Light from a monochromatic source (like a sodium lamp) reflects off both the top and bottom surfaces of this air film. The reflected rays interfere-constructively (bright rings) or destructively (dark rings)-depending on the path difference and phase shift between them. Newton's Rings can be used to calculate the wavelength of monochromatic light, helps determine the radius of curvature of lenses and used in precision optics to detect surface irregularities
